title: Two minutes at the bedside
text:
Mr Kolev was 74 and had been admitted for a routine operation on his hip. Everything went well. The surgery took ninety minutes, there were no complications, and he was due to be discharged on the fourth day.

On the second morning a junior doctor noticed he had stopped eating. His notes said nothing unusual. His blood pressure was normal, the wound was clean, and no test showed a problem.

She sat down for two minutes and asked him why.

He told her he was afraid that if he ate, he would need the toilet, and he couldn't reach it alone, and he didn't want to trouble the nurses. He had decided, quietly, to eat as little as possible until he went home.

The solution took one sentence to a nurse and a call bell moved 30 centimetres closer to his hand.

He ate lunch that day. He was discharged on time and made a full recovery.

Her consultant used the story in teaching for years afterwards. Every test they ran was normal, he would say. The information they needed was not in any of them.

questions.q: Why had Mr Kolev stopped eating?
options: He was afraid of needing the toilet and troubling the nurses
He had lost his appetite after surgery
The food made him feel sick
He was told not to eat before a test
The call bell was moved within his reach
He was moved to another ward

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
options: Talking to the patient can reveal what tests cannot

title: The waiting list
text:
The clinic had a nine-month waiting list for one particular procedure. Patients complained, staff apologised, and everyone assumed the answer was more doctors or more money.

A new manager spent three weeks looking at the data instead. What she found surprised the team.

Around 18% of appointments were no-shows. Another 12% were patients who arrived without the referral letter their GP should have sent, so they were turned away and booked again months later. Together, almost a third of the capacity was being lost before anyone touched a patient.

She made three changes. A text message two days before each appointment. A simple check when booking, confirming the referral was already in the system. And a short list of patients who agreed to come at four hours' notice if a slot opened.

Nothing new was bought and nobody was hired.

Six months later the waiting list was five months, not nine. No-shows had dropped to 7%.

The consultant who had asked for two extra staff put it honestly at the review meeting. He said he had been treating a process problem as a resource problem for three years.

questions.q: What was causing most of the lost capacity?
What is a "no-show" in this text?
options: A patient who books but doesn't attend

questions.q: What resources were added to fix the problem?
options: None; the process was changed instead
He had mistaken a process problem for a resource problem
He had been right all along
